title: OPEC and Middle East Supply Watch
dek: Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries and its allies (OPEC+) quotas, the Middle East supply disruption, Gulf loadings, and Saudi pricing: the state of the world's swing supply.

claims.text: The full OPEC+ ministerial meeting is scheduled for Nov 29, 2026 in Vienna and is expected to consider the capacity audit commissioned from DeGolyer and MacNaughton, which two sources told Reuters in early October had slipped from its original end-September deadline to mid-November, House of Saud reported. The audit will serve as the reference for 2027 production baselines, and the meeting will also need to address the roughly 2 million barrels per day group-wide cut layer that expires on Dec 31, the report said.

OilPrice.com reported on Nov 9 that Iraq's campaign for a larger OPEC production allocation has been complicated by Oil Minister Basim Mohammed Khudair's statement that Iraq is already producing more than 5 million barrels per day (b/d), more than half a million barrels above its OPEC+ requirement of 4.431 million b/d, which Baghdad had agreed six days earlier to maintain for December alongside six other producers. Khudair said Iraq remained compliant because its exports were within an export ceiling, but OPEC+ compliance is assessed on crude production from independent secondary sources, not exports, OilPrice.com noted. Iraq reported production of 4.399 million b/d to OPEC in September, the International Energy Agency estimated September output lower at 4.10 million b/d and Iraqi sustainable capacity at 4.87 million b/d, and Iraq is seeking a future baseline based on capacity of around 6 million b/d as OPEC assesses members' maximum sustainable capacity for its 2027 framework. Iraqi exports rose to about 3.5 million b/d in October from 2.65 million b/d in September, according to Iraqi energy officials cited by Reuters.

Reuters reported on Nov 1 that seven core OPEC+ members, Saudi Arabia, Russia, Iraq, Kuwait, Algeria, Kazakhstan and Oman, kept December production targets steady, the third straight monthly hold since the group completed rolling back the 1.65 million barrel per day cut in September. A separate layer of cuts of about 2 million barrels per day still covers most members through the end of 2026, and all 21 members meet on November 29 to decide 2027 quotas, after a fourth-quarter review of members' production capacity sets the baselines.

Nigeria met its OPEC crude oil production quota for a fifth consecutive month in September, averaging 1.53 million barrels per day against its 1.5 million barrels per day allocation, or 102 percent, according to data released by the Nigerian Upstream Petroleum Regulatory Commission (NUPRC) on Oct 13. Combined crude and condensate output averaged 1,717,030 barrels per day, up 2.34 percent from August, and the regulator attributed the performance to stable operations across most producing assets and the absence of major pipeline outages.

In an Oct 2 exclusive, Reuters reported that OPEC+ has delayed its maximum sustainable capacity (MSC) review to mid-November after the US-Israeli war on Iran disrupted expansion projects across the Middle East and threw estimates of future production potential into uncertainty, citing two sources close to the matter. The review, originally due by end-September 2026, is to be used as the reference for 2027 production baselines; Reuters said US consultant DeGolyer and MacNaughton (covering all members except Russia, Iran and Venezuela) will not submit its report to OPEC until mid-November, a timeline that still allows consideration at the group's next group-wide meeting in late November.

Reuters reported on Oct 4 that the seven core OPEC+ members (Saudi Arabia, Russia, Iraq, Kuwait, Algeria, Kazakhstan and Oman) agreed in a brief online meeting to keep November oil production targets steady, the second straight monthly pause since the unwind of the 2023 voluntary cuts began in April. Reuters noted Gulf OPEC+ producers have been pumping well below targets with exports fluctuating at 60% to 80% of normal levels, and quoted UBS analyst Giovanni Staunovo saying the market consequently remains tight, with Brent crude above $100 a barrel versus about $73 before the Iran war started in late February.

The seven OPEC+ producers that unwound the 2023 voluntary cuts will meet again on October 4, 2026 to set November production levels, keeping the monthly review cadence in place. Independent capacity assessments are due by the end of September, and their results are meant to set the reference production levels that will anchor 2027 quotas. Full ministerial talks on December output policy are expected on November 4, according to OPEC statements.
claims.vintage: OPEC announcement Sep 7, 2026; published Sep 10, 2026; accessed 2026-09-28

claims.text: OPEC+ compliance averaged about 115 percent in September against 119 percent in August, according to a delegate cited by Argus. The figures remain preliminary until confirmed by the Joint Ministerial Monitoring Committee (JMMC), the group's technical body. High compliance in wartime means the restraint is real, but it also means the group has less short-term room to offset further Gulf disruptions.
claims.vintage: Event: Sep 2026; published Sep 24, 2026 (single delegate source, preliminary); accessed 2026-09-28

claims.text: Saudi crude output rebounded to 9.2 million barrels per day (b/d) in October, according to a Bloomberg production survey published Nov 7 and reported by House of Saud, up from 8.3 million b/d in September in the International Energy Agency's October report. The kingdom's December target stays at 10.478 million b/d under the Nov 1 OPEC+ decision, so output remained more than 1 million b/d below target even after the October rebound, the report showed.
claims.source: House of Saud (citing Bloomberg survey and IEA)

claims.text: Reuters reported on Nov 10 that OPEC oil output rose in October, according to a Reuters survey, led by gains in Saudi Arabia, Kuwait and Iraq despite continued constraints on exports. JPMorgan put the global supply surplus at about 1.1 million barrels per day in September, widening to about 1.4 million barrels per day in October, as recovering Middle East flows, rising production elsewhere and weak demand pushed supply above consumption, Reuters said.

Reuters reported on Nov 2 that the United Arab Emirates, six months after leaving OPEC, told the ADIPEC conference in Abu Dhabi that it had increased oil exports despite the Iran war, with energy minister Suhail al-Mazrouei saying exports on occasions had been better than before the war. OPEC figures compiled from secondary sources put UAE crude production at 3.917 million barrels per day (b/d) in September, up 15 percent from February and 470,000 b/d above the OPEC+ quota that would have applied in May had the UAE not left OPEC and OPEC+ on May 1, while the International Energy Agency put total UAE oil output, including condensate and other liquids, at a record 5.3 million b/d in September. Abu Dhabi National Oil Company told Reuters the data in the story was wrong and the report inaccurate, Reuters said.

Reuters columnist Clyde Russell wrote on Nov 2, citing Kpler data, that Asia's crude imports sourced through the Strait of Hormuz rose to 7.42 million barrels per day in October, up 366 percent from the 1.59 million low in April but still well below the 13.06 million average of the three months before the war. Middle East exporters are running tanker transits through the contested strait despite missile and drone attack risk, Russell wrote, drawn by high prices.

OilPrice.com reported on Oct 25, citing Kpler figures reported by Reuters, that October flows out of the Strait of Hormuz averaged 11.7 million barrels per day, up from 9.8 million in September and close to the pre-war average of 14.5 million in February, even as at least 25 ships were reported hit in Hormuz in the first 20 days of October.

OPEC+ posted a sharp gain in production in September, pumping an average of 39.07 million barrels per day, up about 900,000 barrels per day from August, OPEC said in its October Monthly Oil Market Report, Reuters reported on Oct 13. Saudi Arabia told OPEC it pumped 8.372 million barrels per day in September, up more than 2 million barrels per day from August, as Aramco ramped up loadings from Gulf export terminals after an attack on the East-West pipeline disrupted its shipments via the Red Sea. Russia's output fell by 38,000 barrels per day, declining amid Ukrainian strikes on its energy infrastructure.

The US Energy Information Administration raised its Brent forecast in the October Short-Term Energy Outlook, released Oct 6, to an average $105 a barrel in Q4 2026, $14 above the September outlook, citing falling global inventories and tight diesel markets; the agency estimates Middle East crude production shut-ins averaged about 4.5 million barrels per day in Q4 2026, easing to 2.7 million in Q1 2027, and that September shut-ins were the lowest since the war began. For 2026 as a whole Brent is now expected to average $98 a barrel, up 8% from last month's forecast.

Reuters reported on Oct 3 that Iraq's state-owned Oil Tanker Company moved 2 million barrels of Iraqi crude aboard a chartered very large crude carrier through the Strait of Hormuz, in what its director general Ali Qais Abdul Jabbar described on October 3 as the company's first such operation in decades. The move shifts delivery beyond the strait rather than free-on-board at Basra, giving state marketer SOMO greater sales and pricing flexibility; the company is in talks to buy specialized crude tankers to compete with regional shipping companies, and Reuters noted Iraq had previously secured Iranian permission for its tankers to transit the strait.

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said on Sep 25 that Tehran had conveyed a seven-day plan to Washington through Qatari mediators at the United Nations General Assembly: if the US lifted its naval blockade of Iranian ports, waived oil sanctions, released frozen Iranian assets and observed a ceasefire covering the region including Lebanon, Iran would reopen the Strait of Hormuz and resume nuclear talks within seven days. President Trump publicly rejected the proposal on Sep 26, calling it not acceptable; the Wall Street Journal reported he told aides he expects US strikes could resume after November's midterm elections.

French President Emmanuel Macron said on Sep 24 that France will send soldiers, radar systems and defense systems to Saudi Arabia to help protect the Red Sea port city of Yanbu, a key node for Saudi energy exports that has come under Houthi missile attacks. Macron said the deployment was agreed with Riyadh and framed as defensive, not as French involvement in the wider conflict. Saudi Arabia said on Sep 24 its air defenses intercepted six ballistic missiles launched toward the Yanbu and Taif areas.

The US Maritime Administration urged US-flagged commercial vessels to switch off their Automatic Identification System (AIS) transponders when transiting high-risk waters around the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden, under guidance effective Sep 23, and to vary routes and limit electronic transmissions. The advisory follows a resumption of Houthi attacks on commercial shipping, including missile strikes on two tankers off Yanbu in August, and a Houthi-declared ban on Saudi maritime navigation through the Bab el-Mandeb strait announced July 20.
claims.vintage: Guidance effective Sep 23, 2026; published Sep 25, 2026; accessed 2026-09-28

claims.text: OPEC's September Monthly Oil Market Report showed OPEC 12 crude output rising 346,000 barrels per day from July to August, driven by a 664,000 barrel-per-day jump in Iraq that more than offset declines of 399,000 in Iran and 75,000 in Saudi Arabia. OPEC put group spare capacity at 5.066 million barrels per day, with the Big 4's sustained capacity at 21.449 million, reflecting a 600,000 barrel-per-day capacity gain in the United Arab Emirates since 2022. The report also expects US tight oil to grow by only 50,000 barrels per day in 2026 and stay flat in 2027, far below the EIA's projections.
claims.source: Seeking Alpha (citing OPEC Monthly Oil Market Report)

claims.text: OPEC's July 2026 Monthly Oil Market Report showed June secondary-source output of 22.002 million barrels per day, up 3.051 million month on month, but the composition reflects the war: Saudi Arabia produced 6.847 million barrels per day (down 99,000), Iraq 1.970 million (up 446,000), Kuwait 1.452 million (up 880,000), Iran 2.441 million (up 155,000), and the United Arab Emirates 3.809 million (up 1.642 million).
claims.source: Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) Monthly Oil Market Report

claims.text: IndexBox reported on Oct 31, citing Investing.com reporting of European Union Sentinel satellite imagery, that nine very large crude carriers loaded at Saudi Arabia's Persian Gulf export terminals on Wednesday, October 28, the busiest loading day since hostilities began at the end of February, with combined capacity of roughly 18 million barrels. The report cautioned that a single day of loadings does not by itself establish a sustained rise in Saudi exports.
claims.source: IndexBox (citing Investing.com and Sentinel satellite imagery)

claims.text: Reuters columnist Ron Bousso wrote on Oct 22, citing Kpler data, that Middle East oil exports averaged 17.3 million barrels per day so far in October, up from 16.4 million in September and above the 16.9 million average in the two months before the Feb 28 strikes. Flows through the Strait of Hormuz hit 11.7 million barrels per day in October, up from 9.75 million in September, at about 82 percent of pre-war levels.

Lloyd's List reported Oct 6 that September loadings at Middle East Gulf ports rose 50% month on month, 164% above the crisis low, but refined product loadings remain below pre-crisis levels as Middle East refineries operate at reduced rates; Red Sea attacks and refinery outages have pushed more Saudi crude exports through Hormuz, widening the gap between crude and product loadings.

OilPrice.com reported that crude flows through the Strait of Hormuz fell 27% from the prior week's wartime high to 10.1 million barrels per day after a fresh surge in attacks, with Kpler counting just seven commodity carriers transiting the strait on Tuesday, the lowest since late July; the sharpest drop was in vessels doing ship-to-ship transfers in the Gulf of Oman, the workaround Saudi Arabia has relied on to rebuild exports. Between Sep 28 and Oct 2 at least 12 attacks on oil, LNG and LPG tankers were recorded, per Reuters citing the US Navy-led Joint Maritime Information Center, the highest weekly count since the war began.

Reuters reported Oct 6 that Gulf oil flows excluding Iran averaged over 81% of pre-war levels in September, per Vortexa data, with crude and condensate recovering to 91% of pre-war (against a 16.3 million barrel per day pre-war baseline) while refined-fuel exports, including LPG, lagged at 60% of pre-war (7.3 million baseline); Kpler put total September oil exports at 18.6 million barrels per day, and Saudi shipments rose about 4.2 million barrels per day from August to 6.6 million. Vortexa analyst Claire Jungman cautioned that daily flows are considerably more volatile than before the war, so the question is whether recent levels can be sustained; Iranian exports fell to zero under the US blockade.

Reuters reported on Oct 5, citing provisional Kpler ship-tracking data, that Middle East crude exports rose above pre-war levels on four of the final seven days of September, exceeding pre-war levels on September 24 and between September 27 and 29 at 19.5 million to 22.5 million barrels per day, against a pre-war average of 18 million; the 7-day moving average for crude exports stood at 18.5 million barrels per day on October 1. Reuters noted 40% of flows now bypass Hormuz through Saudi and UAE pipelines plus ship-to-ship transfers, while shipping intelligence firm Marisks reported at least seven tanker incidents, including the VLCC Kazimah III reportedly struck on October 1.

Saudi Arabia's crude exports averaged 5.28 million barrels per day over September 1-23, the strongest pace since the conflict began, with about 3.4 million barrels per day loading at Gulf ports, according to Bloomberg ship-tracking data. Analyst Rory Johnston of Commodity Context wrote on Sep 26 that Hormuz oil flows had reached roughly 13.5 million barrels per day on a seven-day average, about two-thirds of prewar levels, citing Kpler data. Kpler separately put total September Middle East oil exports at 12.8 million barrels per day, the highest since the war began in February but still more than 6 million below prewar.

Iraq's Ministry of Oil clarified on Sep 22 that September crude exports are averaging about 2.6 million barrels per day, correcting media reports of 4 million barrels per day that reflected a single day's spike including a State Oil Marketing Organization (SOMO) shipment routed outside the strait. Exports had topped 3 million barrels per day in the first week of September, the highest since the conflict began, but Reuters reported a more than 400,000 barrel-per-day slide over the month. The ministry described the rate as a significant achievement given the continued closure of the Strait of Hormuz.
claims.source: Iraq Business News (citing the Ministry of Oil)

claims.text: Vitol bought at least 25 million barrels of deeply discounted Iraqi crude in September, becoming Iraq's second-largest crude buyer behind the United Arab Emirates' ADNOC at 40 million barrels, two sources told Reuters. Bloomberg reported on Sep 26 that SOMO is now offering last-minute cargoes as traders back out, with sky-high freight adding about 20 dollars a barrel on the Gulf of Oman to East Asia route and SOMO cutting prices on Basrah Medium and Heavy grades in recent tenders.

Reuters reported on Nov 5 that Saudi Aramco cut its December official selling prices (OSPs) for Asia across all grades by $2 a barrel from November, with the pricing document showing Arab Light at a discount of $7.00 a barrel to the Oman/Dubai average, Arab Medium at $8.00 below and Arab Heavy at $9.35 below, the lowest levels since May 2020 during the pandemic. Aramco also cut December prices for Northwest Europe and the Mediterranean by $1 a barrel across all grades and kept prices for the United States unchanged. A Reuters survey had expected Aramco to keep Asia prices unchanged or cut by up to $2 a barrel, citing ample Middle East supplies and weaker spot premiums, and spot premiums for Middle East benchmarks had returned to pre-war levels that week as producers ramped up exports. HSBC raised its fourth-quarter Saudi crude production forecast to 8.3 million barrels per day from 6.3 million, citing a faster than expected export recovery, Reuters reported.

OilPrice.com reported on Oct 27, citing Bloomberg, that Saudi Aramco offered European refiners spot cargoes for late October and November loading at a discount to its official selling prices, loading from Yanbu on the Red Sea or Sidi Kerir in Egypt, weeks after cancelling October term cargoes when an attack shut the East-West pipeline. Aramco also told European refiners they will receive their full contracted November allocations, and traders said the added Saudi supply had already pushed down prices for some crude grades in Europe.

Reuters columnist Ron Bousso wrote on Oct 22 that benchmark tanker rates for a 2 million barrel cargo from the Middle East to China remain near an all-time high of about $1.4 million a day, more than 12 times pre-war levels, and tanker insurance has risen to about 10 percent of cargo value from about 3 percent before the war. Saudi Aramco and Abu Dhabi National Oil Co have responded with large discounts and some delivered-basis sales to secure buyers in China and India.

Saudi Aramco approached traders in mid-October offering additional spot crude oil cargoes for delivery into Europe in late October and into mid-November, three trade sources told Reuters, in a break from its term-only practice with European customers. Saudi Arabia has been ramping up crude flows through its East-West Pipeline to Red Sea export terminals since early October, after drone attacks forced the pipeline's shutdown on September 11, and Poland's Orlen is expected to get at least four October-loading Saudi cargoes, shipping data showed. The volumes could help make up for cargoes European customers missed in September.

Bloomberg corroborated the Saudi November OSP cut, reporting Aramco told Asian refiners to nominate volumes they wish to pick up next month from ports within the Gulf as well as from Yanbu on the Red Sea or the Mediterranean port of Sidi Kerir, in case the closure of the Strait of Hormuz continues; JPMorgan estimated Middle East crude exports were at 98% of pre-war levels last week, framing the Asia price cut as a bid for market share as flows recover.

Reuters reported on Nov 10 that the global oil market is showing signs of a return to excess supply as demand drops because of high prices, with JPMorgan estimating the global surplus at about 1.4 million barrels per day in October. The dated Brent physical benchmark, against which roughly two thirds of oil supply is priced, has also weakened in recent weeks, Reuters said.

OPEC lowered its forecast for 2026 oil demand growth for a sixth straight month in its October Monthly Oil Market Report, to 180,000 barrels per day from 380,000, putting world demand at 105.72 million barrels per day, Reuters reported on Oct 13. The group raised its 2027 forecast to growth of 2.55 million barrels per day, to an average of 108.3 million barrels per day, assuming demand softens this year as expected and is then bolstered by the need to replenish inventories depleted by the Iran war.

The International Energy Agency's (IEA) October Oil Market Report, released Oct 14, sits far below OPEC's view: global oil demand is predicted to fall 2.6 million barrels per day on average in 2026, with diesel expected to account for 25 percent of the decline, the Associated Press reported. Global production climbed 2.5 million barrels per day month over month to 102.3 million barrels per day in September, driven by Gulf producers, with OPEC+ gains of 2.1 million barrels per day led by Saudi Arabia. The agency expects supply to drop by 5.8 million barrels per day to 100.7 million barrels per day this year and said renewed Gulf attacks leave the recovery fragile.

OPEC's September 2026 Monthly Oil Market Report cut its 2026 oil demand growth forecast for the fifth straight month, lowering it by 200,000 barrels per day to 380,000, with total consumption at 105.84 million barrels per day; it raised the 2027 growth forecast to 2.36 million barrels per day and noted July OPEC+ output of 38.055 million barrels per day.

The United Arab Emirates withdrew from OPEC and OPEC+ effective May 1, 2026, according to the September report, which also cut cumulative 2026 demand growth by about 1 million barrels per day since the US-Iran war began.
